content.content:
1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, bounded
10	  `loop`, and dynamic `map` nodes;
11	- a workflow may declare named versions: every declared version is kept and
12	  each execution is bound to the version that was current (or explicitly
13	  named) when it started, so upgrading a workflow never changes a running
14	  execution, and a running execution can be explicitly migrated to another
15	  version of the same workflow, after which it advances under that version;
16	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
17	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
18	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
19	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
20	  execution;
21	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
22	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
23	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
24	  execution with reason `rejected`);
25	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
26	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
27	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
28	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
29	- a map node inside a loop body expands independently in every iteration
30	  from that iteration's source output, its instances and events belonging
31	  to the iteration they expanded in;
32	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
33	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
34	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
35	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
36	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
37	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
38	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
39	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
40	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
41	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
42	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
43	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
44	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
45	- subscriptions may also declare queue targets instead of webhook addresses:
46	  matching business events are appended, in occurrence order, to persistent
47	  per-execution queues that callers pull from and acknowledge explicitly,
48	  with a visibility timeout returning unacknowledged messages to the pending
49	  set (delivery is at least once);
50	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
51	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
52	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
53	  resumed, periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
54	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy, and a read-only preview
55	  query projects the upcoming trigger times and their inputs.
56	
57	## Requirements
58	
59	- Python 3.11 or newer
60	- no third-party runtime dependencies
61	
62	## Run the service
63	
64	```bash
65	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
66	```
67	
68	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
69	has bound the port.
70	
71	## HTTP API
72	
73	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
74	
75	Responses are compact JSON with no insignificant whitespace, and every
76	response body ends with exactly one trailing newline (`\n`). Numbers
77	round-trip with their full precision: finite floats keep their original
78	IEEE-754 value through the shortest textual representation that decodes to
79	it (so `0.30000000000000004` stays `0.30000000000000004`), negative zero is
80	preserved as `-0.0`, and integers stay integers. Non-finite numbers may
81	never appear in a request and are never produced in a response; timestamps
82	are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in `Z`.
83	
84	### Tenants and quotas
85	
86	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
87	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
88	delivery history, and queue record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
89	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
90	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
91	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
92	example advancing, migrating, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
93	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, queues, or schedule of an execution or
94	workflow owned by another tenant, or pulling from or acknowledging one of its
95	queues — is answered exactly like a reference to a
96	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
97	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
98	workflow of the same tenant, and a migration can only name a version of that
99	workflow in the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier or
100	version is the usual `404 not_found`.
101	
102	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
103	including creation, advancement, migration, approval decisions, lease
104	operations, cancellation, recovery, replay, instance deletion and
105	modification and re-expansion, queue pulls, acknowledgements, and all
106	history and status queries, as well as the usage, bill, and metrics queries. An empty
107	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
108	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
109	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
110	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
111	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
112	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
113	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
114	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
115	the usual `409 conflict`.
116	
117	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
118	hold:
119	
120	```http
121	PUT /quotas
122	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
123	X-Tenant-Id: acme
124	
125	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
126	```
127	
128	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
129	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer; a non-positive,
130	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
131	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Both quota
132	routes require a tenant: calling them without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
133	one) is a `400 validation_error`. The response is
134	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
135	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
136	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
137	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
138	
139	```http
140	GET /quotas
141	X-Tenant-Id: acme
142	```
143	
144	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
145	when the tenant has declared none.
146	
147	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the whole request is
148	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
149	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
150	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
151	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write: nothing is inserted and
152	previously stored data is unaffected, exactly as for validation failures.
153	
154	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
155	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
156	is at its execution limit, the due period creates no execution and the
157	schedule is left unchanged — its cursor, `last_triggered_at`, and
158	`last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the period is settled on a later
159	pass once capacity exists, under the usual per-period idempotence. Delivery
160	history follows the tenant of the execution it belongs to.
161	
162	### Usage metering and billing
163	
164	Requests that carry a tenant identifier leave a usage record for each billable
165	action they perform. Only tenant-scoped requests are metered: a request that
166	omits the `X-Tenant-Id` header keeps the legacy namespace and writes no usage
167	record at all, with its state shapes and event content unchanged. The four
168	metered action types are:
169	
170	- `workflow_created` — a workflow definition is stored. Adding a new version
171	  to an existing workflow is one workflow creation, the same as the first
172	  definition;
173	- `execution_started` — an execution is created and starts `running`;
174	- `schedule_triggered` — a due schedule period creates its execution. The
175	  scheduled execution is metered both as `execution_started` and as
176	  `schedule_triggered`;
177	- `delivery_attempted` — one outbound webhook HTTP attempt is made, or one
178	  queue message is delivered to a caller pulling from a queue. A
179	  subscription that retries is metered once per attempt, so a delivery that
180	  fails and then succeeds on its second attempt records two attempts; the
181	  action is metered whether it ultimately succeeds or fails. A queue pull
182	  meters one attempt per message it delivers, so a redelivery after the
183	  visibility timeout is metered again, while a pull that delivers nothing
184	  meters nothing.
185	
186	Metering is atomic with the action it describes: a write rejected by
187	validation or by a quota produces no record and performs no partial write.
188	Repeating an idempotent command returns its first result and writes no second
189	record, and settling the same schedule period more than once (a repeated
190	trigger or a later pass) meters that period only once. Replay, recovery, and
191	queries never meter and never alter recorded usage or billing conclusions.
192	
193	```http
194	GET /usage
195	X-Tenant-Id: acme
196	```
197	
198	Returns `{"usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}`: the
199	cumulative count of recorded actions per type, sorted by ascending type
200	identifier. Types with no records are omitted, so a tenant with no usage gets
201	the definite empty result `{"usage":[]}`.
202	
203	```http
204	GET /bill
205	X-Tenant-Id: acme
206	```
207	
208	Returns the per-type bill:
209	
210	```json
211	{"bill":{"items":[
212	  {"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100},
213	  {"type":"workflow_created","count":2,"unit_price":1000,"subtotal":2000}
214	],"total":2100}}
215	```
216	
217	Each item gives the metered `count`, a positive-integer `unit_price` in cents
218	that is also returned in the response, and a `subtotal` equal to
219	`count * unit_price`; `total` is the integer-cent sum of every subtotal. With
220	no records, `items` is empty and `total` is `0`.
221	
222	Both endpoints accept the same two optional query parameters the events and
223	metrics queries accept, each an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp ending in `Z`:
224	
225	```http
226	GET /usage?since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
227	GET /bill?since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
228	X-Tenant-Id: acme
229	```
230	
231	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on each usage record's
232	  occurrence time: a record whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted.
233	  When either parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting
234	  both returns exactly the cumulative result above;
235	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
236	  parameter is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing;
237	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
238	  simply contains no records. Usage then reports the definite empty result
239	  `{"usage":[]}`, and the bill reports an empty `items` list with a `total` of
240	  `0`.
241	
242	Only records whose occurrence time falls in the window are counted. Within
243	the window the bill keeps the same basis as always: each present type reports
244	its windowed count, its usual `unit_price`, and a `subtotal` of the two; items
245	stay sorted by ascending type identifier, and a type with no record in the
246	window is omitted rather than reported at zero. The query is read-only: it
247	writes no usage records, changes no prices or metering conclusions, and never
248	alters already recorded usage — under event replay or recovery the same window
249	always gives the same answer.
250	
251	Both endpoints are tenant-scoped `GET` requests: a missing or empty
252	`X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error` that reveals no usage. Usage and
253	bill data follow the usual tenant isolation, so one tenant can never see
254	another's records in any window, and another tenant's records never affect
255	this tenant's counts or totals.
256	
257	### Per-record usage history
258	
259	The cumulative usage query reports only per-type totals. A separate endpoint
260	returns the individual usage records themselves, so each billed action can be
261	checked against the moment it occurred:
262	
263	```http
264	GET /usage/records?limit=50
265	X-Tenant-Id: acme
266	```
267	
268	Returns `{"records":[...]}` with the matching records in ascending order of
269	occurrence time; records sharing one instant are ordered by ascending
270	sequence. Each record is:
271	
272	```json
273	{"sequence":7,"type":"execution_started","occurred_at":"2026-09-26T08:30:00.000Z"}
274	```
275	
276	- `sequence` is a stable, strictly increasing positive integer per tenant. It
277	  identifies the record across every query and is never renumbered by a
278	  filter or a page;
279	- `type` is the metered action type;
280	- `occurred_at` is the record's occurrence time as an ISO-8601 UTC string
281	  ending in `Z`.
282	
283	A tenant with no matching records gets the definite empty result
284	`{"records":[]}`, never an error. The response ends with a single newline,
285	like every other JSON endpoint.
286	
287	The endpoint accepts the same optional closed time window the events and
288	usage queries accept, plus cursor pagination:
289	
290	```http
291	GET /usage/records?since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
292	```
293	
294	- `since` and `until` are ISO-8601 UTC timestamps ending in `Z` and bind a
295	  **closed** interval on each record's occurrence time: a record whose time
296	  equals either boundary is included. When either is absent the corresponding
297	  bound is open; when `since` is later than `until` the window matches
298	  nothing and the definite empty list is returned;
299	- `limit` is **required** and must be a positive integer; a page never
300	  contains more than that many records;
301	- `cursor` is the `sequence` of the previous page's last record; only records
302	  whose `sequence` is strictly greater are returned, so pages neither overlap
303	  nor skip. It is omitted on the first page and must be a positive integer;
304	- the time window and pagination apply together as an intersection, and
305	  filtering never changes a record's `sequence`.
306	
307	A malformed timestamp, a missing or non-positive-integer `limit`, a
308	non-positive-integer `cursor`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
309	parameter is a `400 validation_error`. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a
310	`400 validation_error` that reveals no records. The query is read-only: it
311	appends no usage records, writes no events, and changes no metering, prices,
312	quotas, or billing conclusions. Records follow the usual tenant isolation, so
313	another tenant's records are never visible under any window or page and never
314	affect this tenant's result; replay and recovery leave every recorded
315	sequence, time, and billing conclusion unchanged.
316	
317	### Operational metrics
318	
319	```http
320	GET /metrics
321	X-Tenant-Id: acme
322	```
323	
324	Returns one line of compact JSON summarizing the business facts already
325	recorded for the tenant, ending with the usual single newline. The endpoint
326	is read-only: it appends no events, writes no usage records, and changes no
327	stored data, and it reports only persisted facts — it performs no
328	advancement, approval, recovery, or replay of its own, so those operations
329	never change what a metrics query observes beyond the facts they themselves
330	recorded. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`, and
331	the metrics follow the usual tenant isolation: another tenant's facts are
332	never visible in any dimension and never affect this tenant's counts. A
333	tenant with no recorded facts at all gets the definite empty result with
334	every dimension at zero — not an error. With no query parameters the answer
335	is every fact recorded for the tenant, byte for byte.
336	
337	The query accepts two optional query parameters, each an ISO-8601 UTC
338	timestamp ending in `Z`:
339	
340	```http
341	GET /metrics?since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
342	X-Tenant-Id: acme
343	```
344	
345	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on the facts' occurrence
346	  times: a fact whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted. When either
347	  parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting both
348	  counts every recorded fact;
349	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
350	  parameter is a `400 validation_error`;
351	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
352	  simply contains no facts, so every dimension reports its definite zero
353	  result.
354	
355	Each dimension is windowed by the occurrence time of its own fact: node
356	completions, failures, and retry consumption use the time of their recorded
357	node events; delivery outcomes use the delivery record's `occurred_at`
358	(shared by every attempt recorded in it); schedule triggers use the settled
359	period's trigger time; and the status distribution counts an execution at
360	the time it entered its current status — a still-running execution at its
361	start time, and a completed or terminated execution at the time of its
362	completion or termination event.
363	
364	### Export metrics in Prometheus text format
365	
366	```http
367	GET /metrics/export
368	X-Tenant-Id: acme
369	```
370	
371	A read-only tenant-scoped entry point that returns the same counts as the
372	metrics query — including the same optional `since` and `until` filters, the
373	same closed-interval semantics, the same definite zero result for a window
374	with `since` later than `until`, and the same `400 validation_error` for a
375	missing or empty tenant, a malformed timestamp, or an unknown query
376	parameter — rendered in the Prometheus text exposition format
377	(`text/plain; version=0.0.4`). It writes no events and no usage records.
378	
379	Each top-level metrics dimension is one metric family named with the
380	dimension's public key prefixed by `chronicleflow_`. The families appear in
381	the documented top-level key order, and the samples within a family are
382	ordered by ascending label value:
383	
384	- `chronicleflow_status_distribution` — samples carry a `status` label
385	  (`running`, `completed`, `terminated`); only the terminated samples also
386	  carry a `reason` label naming one of the four termination reasons;
387	- `chronicleflow_node_completions`, `chronicleflow_node_failures`, and
388	  `chronicleflow_retry_consumption` — samples carry a `node` label;
389	- `chronicleflow_schedule_triggers` — samples carry a `workflow` label;
390	- `chronicleflow_delivery_succeeded` and `chronicleflow_delivery_failed` —
391	  unlabeled scalar samples.
392	
393	Every value is a decimal integer. A dimension with no facts in the window
394	still exposes a zero-valued sample line (the labeled families expose one
395	unlabeled `0` sample). Every line ends with a newline and the whole document
396	ends with a single newline.
397	
398	The top-level keys appear in this order — status distribution, node
399	completions, node failures, retry consumption, delivery successes, delivery
400	failures, and schedule triggers:
401	
402	```json
403	{"status_distribution":{"running":1,"completed":2,"terminated":{"cancelled":0,"rejected":1,"retries_exhausted":0,"timeout":0}},"node_completions":{"charge":3},"node_failures":{"charge":2},"retry_consumption":{"charge":1},"delivery_succeeded":4,"delivery_failed":1,"schedule_triggers":{"nightly-orders":2}}
404	```
405	
406	- `status_distribution` — the tenant's executions divided into `running`,
407	  `completed`, and `terminated`; `terminated` is further broken down by
408	  termination reason, with every reason (`cancelled`, `rejected`,
409	  `retries_exhausted`, `timeout`) always present, zero when no execution
410	  ended for that reason.
411	- `node_completions` — persisted node completion facts per node identifier.
412	  Condition evaluations and skips are not completions and are never counted;
413	  a loop body node counts once per iteration it completes.
414	- `node_failures` — submitted task failures per node identifier; a loop body
415	  node accumulates each iteration's failures.
416	- `retry_consumption` — the number of times a failed task was re-queued for
417	  another attempt, per node identifier.
418	- `delivery_succeeded` and `delivery_failed` — outbound delivery attempts by
419	  outcome. Every attempt counts exactly once, so a delivery that fails and
420	  then succeeds on a later attempt records one of each.
421	- `schedule_triggers` — schedule periods that created an execution, per
422	  workflow identifier; settling the same period again counts nothing more.
423	
424	All counts are non-negative integers. A dimension with no facts reports zero
425	(or an empty group) rather than being omitted, and the groups within a
426	dimension are ordered by ascending identifier. Migrating an execution to
427	another version does not change attribution: facts recorded before and after
428	the migration accumulate under the same names. The optional `since` and
429	`until` filters and the Prometheus text export are described above.

432	
433	```http
434	GET /health
435	```
436	
437	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.

439	### Create a workflow
440	
441	```http
442	POST /workflows
443	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
444	
445	{
446	  "id": "order-flow",
447	  "nodes": [
448	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
449	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
450	  ]
451	}
452	```
453	
454	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
455	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
456	
457	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
458	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
459	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
460	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
461	
462	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
463	
464	```json
465	{
466	  "id": "order-flow",
467	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
468	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
469	}
470	```
471	
472	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
473	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
474	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
475	
476	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
477	
478	```json
479	{
480	  "id": "nightly-orders",
481	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
482	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
483	}
484	```
485	
486	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
487	
488	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
489	
490	```json
491	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
492	```
493	
494	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
495	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
496	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
497	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
498	`false`.
499	
500	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
501	
502	```json
503	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
504	```
505	
506	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
507	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
508	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
509	dependencies of its successors.
510	
511	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
512	
513	```json
514	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
515	```
516	
517	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
518	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
519	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
520	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
521	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
522	`retries_exhausted`.
523	
524	A task may instead declare an approval point:
525	
526	```json
527	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
528	```
529	
530	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
531	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
532	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
533	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
534	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
535	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
536	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
537	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
538	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
539	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
540	move the task.
541	
542	### Submit an approval decision
543	
544	```http
545	POST /executions/run-1/decision
546	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
547	
548	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
549	```
550	
551	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
552	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
553	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
554	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
555	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
556	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
557	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
558	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
559	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
560	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
561	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
562	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
563	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
564	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
565	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
566	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
567	404.
568	
569	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
570	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
571	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
572	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
573	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
574	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
575	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
576	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
577	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
578	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
579	shape and event stream.
580	
581	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
582	segment:
583	
584	```json
585	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
586	```
587	
588	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
589	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
590	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
591	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the repeated segment anchored by
592	the entry task and the condition: it is the entry task, the condition, and
593	every node either anchor reaches through `depends_on`. The two anchors must
594	be connected — the condition gates the entry task (the entry depends on it)
595	or the condition is evaluated after the entry task (it depends on the entry),
596	as in the example above. The body keeps the usual DAG rules and always
597	contains the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
598	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
599	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
600	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
601	loop node instead).
602	
603	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
604	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
605	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
606	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
607	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
608	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
609	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
610	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
611	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
612	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
613	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
614	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors. Once the loop
615	has finished, the execution-level `completed_nodes` list also includes every
616	body node that completed in any iteration, each listed only once and in the
617	order of its first completion, followed by the loop node itself; body nodes
618	skipped by a `run_if` guard remain out of the execution-level completed list
619	and are visible only in their iteration record. Body task outputs still
620	belong only to their iterations.
621	
622	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
623	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
624	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
625	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
626	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
627	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
628	exactly.
629	
630	### Dynamic map nodes
631	
632	A `map` node expands at runtime into one task instance per element of a
633	recorded array:
634	
635	```json
636	{"id": "ship", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["collect"],
637	 "source": "collect", "path": "items", "max_instances": 100,
638	 "template": {"id": "ship-item", "retries": 2}}
639	```
640	
641	A map node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `source`, `path`,
642	`max_instances`, and `template`; any other field is rejected as unknown.
643	
644	- `source` names a `task` node that is also listed in `depends_on`. Expansion
645	  begins only after every dependency has completed or been skipped; the
646	  element list comes solely from the source task's recorded output.
647	- `path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into that recorded output, using
648	  the same path syntax as a condition.
649	- `max_instances` is a positive integer bounding how many elements may
650	  expand.
651	- `template` describes the single task each instance runs and contains
652	  exactly an `id`, and optionally `retries` (an integer between 0 and 10,
653	  defaulting to 0) and an `approval` point with the same shape a task node
654	  uses. The template id only names the dynamically expanded instances; it
655	  may coincide with a declared node id or with another map's template id.
656	  A map node may also sit inside a loop body, expanding independently in
657	  every iteration (see "Maps inside loop bodies" below).
658	
659	When the dependencies settle, the value at `path` is read once. When it is an
660	array, one instance is created per element; the instances queue in ascending
661	element index order. Each `advance` still settles exactly one ready item, so
662	instances are worked in index order, one per call. An instance is an ordinary
663	task in every other respect: a submitted failure consumes the template's
664	retry bound and re-queues that instance, and a template approval point parks
665	the execution with the instance's `map_id` and `index` recorded, until an
666	approver decides it. Retries and approvals are per instance: results never
667	overwrite another instance.
668	
669	When every instance is completed, the map node completes and its output,
670	recorded both in the node's `outputs` entry and under its `maps` record, is
671	the list of instance outputs in ascending element order; its successors then
672	become available in the usual way.
673	
674	A value that is missing or is not an array expands to zero instances: the map
675	completes with an empty output list and releases its successors immediately.
676	When the array holds more elements than `max_instances`, no instance is
677	created at all: the map node fails permanently, is listed under
678	`failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`
679	under the usual exhaustion semantics.
680	
681	Execution state exposes each map under `maps`: the node's `status`
682	(`pending`, `running`, `completed`, or `failed`), one record per retained
683	instance giving its `index`, `status` (`ready`, `waiting`, `completed`, or
684	`failed`), its `output`, and its `failure_reason` (null except for a
685	permanently failed instance), plus the ordered completed `outputs` list and
686	the node's single `failure_reason`. A `ready` instance that has been
687	rewritten by a successful modify additionally carries that rewritten
688	`input`; every other instance record keeps exactly these fields. The `maps`
689	field is present only when the bound workflow declares a map node outside
690	any loop body; every other execution keeps its previous state shape.
691	
692	The event stream records a `map_expanded` event when expansion happens,
693	carrying the map id and the number of created instances (zero for a missing
694	or non-array value, and zero together with `exceeded` and the observed
695	element count when the bound is exceeded), and a `map_completed` event with
696	the map id and final instance count. Each instance's per-node events —
697	`node_completed`, `node_failed`, and `node_retried`, plus
698	`approval_requested` and `approval_decided` for a template approval point —
699	carry their `map_id` and element `index` alongside the template node id, so
700	replay rebuilds every instance solely from the event stream. Checkpoints are
701	written at instance boundaries, so recovery resumes with the unfinished
702	instances and never repeats an instance output. Per-instance completions and
703	failures count toward the existing node metrics under the template node id,
704	and webhook and queue subscriptions receive instance events exactly like any
705	other node event. Instance deletion and modification add their own
706	`instance_deleted` and `instance_modified` events, and re-expansion adds a
707	`map_reexpanded` event, described under
708	"Delete and modify expanded instances" below.
709	
710	### Maps inside loop bodies
711	
712	A map node may belong to a loop body — it is part of the body exactly when
713	the loop's entry or condition reaches it through `depends_on`, like any
714	other body member:
715	
716	```json
717	{"id": "fanout", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["attempt"],
718	 "source": "attempt", "path": "items", "max_instances": 10,
719	 "template": {"id": "work", "retries": 1}}
720	```
721	
722	A nested map expands once per iteration, when every dependency of its node
723	is completed or skipped in that iteration, and the element list is read from
724	the source task's output of that same iteration. The expansion rules are the
725	ones of an execution-level map: a missing path or a non-array value expands
726	to zero instances and the map completes for that iteration with an empty
727	output list, so the loop boundary is evaluated as usual; an element count
728	beyond `max_instances` creates no instance at all — the map fails
729	permanently, is listed under `failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates
730	with reason `retries_exhausted` under the usual exhaustion semantics.
731	
732	The expanded instances belong to their iteration only: they queue in
733	ascending element index order and are settled one per `advance`, exactly
734	like execution-level instances, and one iteration's instances never
735	overwrite another iteration's results. An instance is an ordinary task in
736	every other respect — a submitted failure consumes the template's retry
737	bound and re-queues that instance within its iteration, and a template
738	approval point parks the execution until an approver decides it — with no
739	influence from the iteration number.
740	
741	Iteration state exposes each nested map under the iteration record's `maps`
742	field, with the same per-map shape as an execution-level map (`status`, one
743	record per instance, the ordered completed `outputs`, and `failure_reason`);
744	the field is present on every iteration of a loop whose body declares a map
745	node. When a nested map completes, its node enters the iteration's
746	`completed_nodes` and its output list is recorded in the iteration's
747	`outputs`; when the loop finishes, the usual roll-up lists the map node once
748	in the execution-level `completed_nodes`, while its outputs stay with their
749	iterations. An execution-level `maps` field is not created for nested maps.
750	
751	Every event a nested expansion records carries the owning `loop_id` and
752	`iteration` alongside the map id and, for per-instance events, the element
753	`index`: `map_expanded`, `map_completed`, the per-instance `node_completed`,
754	`node_failed`, and `node_retried`, and `approval_requested` and
755	`approval_decided` for a template approval point. The `iteration_started`
756	event of a loop whose body declares map nodes carries the iteration's
757	initial `maps` skeleton, so replay rebuilds every iteration's instance list,
758	status, and ownership solely from the event stream, consistent with the
759	materialized state. Checkpoints are written at each iteration's instance
760	boundaries, so recovery continues the current iteration's unfinished
761	instances and never repeats an instance output. Cancellation, timeouts,
762	leases, retries, and approvals keep their existing semantics, and a nested
763	map never changes an execution's termination reason.
764	
765	Executions whose workflows declare no nested map behave exactly as before:
766	state fields, event contents, and advancement results are unchanged.
767	
768	### Delete and modify expanded instances
769	
770	An expanded dynamic node offers, alongside expansion and per-instance
771	advancement, two instance-level operations and a node-level re-expansion.
772	All three are ordinary idempotent HTTP commands over the same entry points
773	the rest of the service uses; they introduce no second protocol.
774	
775	An instance that has never advanced can be removed, and so can an instance
776	that has permanently failed:
777	
778	```http
779	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/2/delete
780	Idempotency-Key: delete-instance-2
781	
782	{}
783	```
784	
785	The body must be an empty object. Removing an instance drops only that
786	instance's record: every retained instance keeps its element index, its
787	place in the queue, and its advancement order. When the removed instance was
788	the map's last unfinished instance, the node completes under the existing
789	rules with an output list containing only the retained instances' outputs,
790	in ascending element-index order, and its successors unlock as usual. An
791	instance that is waiting on an approval, or has already completed, can never
792	be deleted; attempting it returns `409 conflict` and changes no state. A
793	permanently failed instance is removable after the execution has terminated,
794	but removing it never revives the execution, alters its termination reason,
795	or changes the node's failed conclusion. When every retained instance of a
796	map inside a loop body has ended, the iteration's other nodes advance as
797	usual and the node completes or ends under the existing rules; deleting an
798	instance in one iteration never touches another iteration.
799	
800	An instance that has never advanced can also have its input rewritten
801	before it is worked:
802	
803	```http
804	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/1/modify
805	Idempotency-Key: modify-instance-1
806	
807	{"input":{"address":"742 Evergreen Terrace"}}
808	```
809	
810	The body must contain exactly `input`, an object with the new content; it is
811	validated like every other request body (finite numbers only). The rewrite
812	changes only the parameters used when that one instance is later advanced:
813	it affects no other instance, and the output and history of an instance that
814	has already advanced (waiting, completed, or permanently failed) are
815	immutable — modifying such an instance returns `409 conflict` and changes no
816	state. The rewritten input, including its full float precision and `-0.0`,
817	is stored verbatim.
818	
819	Delete and modify calls on the same instance settle in call order: every
820	call applies to the instance list exactly as the earlier calls left it, and
821	several calls on one instance each take effect independently, one after
822	another. A rewritten instance has still never advanced, so it remains
823	deletable; deleting or modifying an instance an earlier call already
824	removed is a `404 not_found`; and a second rewrite of the same instance
825	records the first rewrite's content as its `before`.
826	
827	Both commands apply to a map nested in a loop body exactly as to an
828	execution-level map: the current running iteration's instances are
829	addressed by the same path, and every event they append carries the owning
830	`loop_id` and `iteration` alongside the map id; an execution-level instance
831	carries no loop context.
832	
833	An out-of-bounds element index, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic
834	`map`, a missing execution, or a cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found`
835	and writes nothing. A missing or mistyped field, a non-object modify
836	`input`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a `400 validation_error`
837	with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a
838	`409 conflict`; repeating the same command with the same key returns the
839	first result and appends no second event.
840	
841	Every successful call appends exactly one event to the execution stream:
842	
843	- an `instance_deleted` event records the action type, the owning dynamic
844	  node under `map_id`, the removed instance's element `index` and `status`
845	  (`ready` or `failed`), and, for a map inside a loop body, the `loop_id`
846	  and `iteration`;
847	- an `instance_modified` event records the action type, the owning
848	  `map_id`, the instance `index`, the content `before` the rewrite (`null`
849	  for an instance that had never been rewritten) and `after` it, and the
850	  same loop context when the instance belongs to an iteration.
851	
852	Replay rebuilds the instance list, every instance's status and ownership,
853	and each rewrite solely from the event stream: a delete drops the recorded
854	instance (and the subsequent `map_completed`, when the deletion finished the
855	node, completes it with the retained outputs), and a modify applies the
856	rewritten input to that one instance, so the rebuilt state is exactly the
857	materialized state. A checkpoint is written at the instance boundary of
858	every successful delete or modify; after a restart recovery continues the
859	unfinished instances, repeats no instance output, and never resurrects a
860	deleted instance. The operations change no advancement conclusion or
861	termination semantics: cancellation, timeouts, approvals, leases, retries,
862	and retry exhaustion keep their existing behavior. Executions that never
863	use deletion, modification, or re-expansion keep exactly their current
864	state fields, event contents, and advancement results.
865	
866	### Re-expand a dynamic node
867	
868	A dynamic node that has already expanded can be expanded again on demand —
869	above all to regenerate its instance list after deletions:
870	
871	```http
872	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/reexpand
873	Idempotency-Key: reexpand-1
874	
875	{}
876	```
877	
878	(The same operation is also accepted at `.../maps/ship/expand`.) The body
879	must be an empty object. Re-expansion reads the element list again from the
880	source task's recorded output — the same recorded output the first
881	expansion read, which never changes once recorded — and regenerates the
882	instance list from it: every previous instance record is replaced, and the
883	fresh instances queue from element index zero in ascending order. The
884	regenerated instances are ordinary instances in every respect: they are
885	deleted, modified, advanced, retried, and approved through the same entries
886	and with exactly the same behavior as a first expansion, and their retry
887	bounds start from zero.
888	
889	Every successful call appends exactly one `map_reexpanded` event, recording
890	the action type, the owning dynamic node under `map_id`, and the number of
891	generated instances under `instance_count`; for a map inside a loop body
892	the event also carries the owning `loop_id` and `iteration`, and only the
893	current running iteration's expansion is replaced. A node that had
894	completed returns to `running`: it leaves `completed_nodes`, its recorded
895	output entry is discarded, and when the regenerated instances have all
896	completed the node completes again under the existing rules, its result
897	list holding only the finally retained instances' outputs in ascending
898	element-index order. An empty element list completes the node again at
899	once with an empty output list, exactly like a zero-element first
900	expansion.
901	
902	Re-expansion is rejected with `409 conflict` and writes nothing when the
903	node has not expanded yet, when it has permanently failed, when one of its
904	instances is waiting on an approval decision, when the execution has
905	already completed, or when a nested map's loop is not currently running.
906	A terminated execution's unfinished node may still be re-expanded; doing so
907	never revives the execution or alters its termination reason. A missing
908	execution, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic `map`, or a
909	cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found` and writes nothing. A
910	non-empty or non-object body, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
911	`400 validation_error` with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key
912	from another operation is a `409 conflict`; repeating the same call with
913	the same key returns the first result and appends no second event. Replay
914	rebuilds the regenerated instance list, statuses, and ownership solely
915	from the event stream, a checkpoint is written at the re-expansion
916	boundary, and recovery after a restart continues the unfinished
917	regenerated instances — repeating no instance output and never resurrecting
918	an instance that stayed deleted.
919	
920	### Workflow versions
921	
922	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
923	
924	```json
925	{
926	  "id": "order-flow",
927	  "version": "2026-09-25",
928	  "nodes": [
929	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
930	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
931	  ]
932	}
933	```
934	
935	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
936	like every other identifier. Posting it when the workflow does not yet exist
937	creates the workflow with that version; posting another definition with a new
938	`version` to the same `id` adds a new version without touching the previous
939	ones — the workflow keeps its entire history, and every stored version remains
940	usable. The most recently added version becomes the workflow's current
941	version. Posting a definition without a `version` to an existing workflow
942	still conflicts, and reusing a version tag already stored for the same
943	workflow is a `409 conflict`; either rejection writes nothing.
944	
945	A version declaration may also carry `subscriptions` and a `schedule`,
946	validated exactly like at creation. Subscriptions are attached to the
947	declared version and apply only to executions bound to it; a version without
948	subscriptions replaces none, and other versions' subscriptions stay intact.
949	Declaring a `schedule` on an added version replaces the workflow's single
950	schedule plan in the usual way (re-anchored, pause flag kept).
951	
952	An execution created without an explicit `version` binds to the workflow's
953	current version at the moment it starts:
954	
955	```http
956	POST /executions
957	Idempotency-Key: execution-versioned
958	
959	{"id":"run-v2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{}}
960	```
961	
962	An execution may instead name the version it wants:
963	
964	```json
965	{"id":"run-v1","workflow_id":"order-flow","version":"2026-08-01","input":{}}
966	```
967	
968	Naming a version that does not exist for the workflow is a missing-resource
969	`404 not_found`, exactly like naming a workflow that does not exist; the
970	execution is not created. Everything about an execution follows its bound
971	version: ready-node selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval
972	points, retry counts, leases, and the subscriptions that fire for its events.
973	Adding a new version never interrupts an execution already running: an
974	execution started before the upgrade keeps advancing on its old version to
975	completion or termination. Its checkpoints are snapshots of the same state,
976	recovery rebuilds from the bound version, and replay rebuilds state and the
977	version binding solely from its event stream; recorded events and historical
978	conclusions never change.
979	
980	A versioned execution's state carries its `version` tag, and its
981	`execution_started` event records the same tag; querying it therefore shows
982	which version it is bound to. A workflow that never declares a version, and an
983	execution of one, keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
984	stream with no added field.
985	
986	The definition query lists every version and the current one:
987	
988	```http
989	GET /workflows/order-flow
990	```
991	
992	```json
993	{"current_version":"2026-09-25","id":"order-flow","versions":[
994	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-08-01"},
995	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-09-25"}
996	]}
997	```
998	
999	Versions are returned in declaration order; each entry is the stored
1000	definition with its `version` tag. A workflow that never declared a version
1001	returns a single untagged entry and `current_version: null`. A missing
1002	workflow returns 404 `not_found`. Cross-tenant references are missing
1003	resources as usual.
1004	
1005	### Migrate a running execution to another version
1006	
1007	```http
1008	POST /executions/run-v1/migrate
1009	Idempotency-Key: migrate-request-1
1010	
1011	{"version":"2026-09-25"}
1012	```
1013	
1014	A running execution can be explicitly moved to another declared version of
1015	the same workflow; after the call it keeps advancing under the new version.
1016	The body must contain exactly `version`, a non-empty version identifier that
1017	names a stored version of the execution's workflow. On success a
1018	`version_migrated` event is appended to the event stream — it records the
1019	`from_version`, the `to_version`, and the structural skeleton of the target
1020	revision (its `loops`, and, when it declares approval points, its
1021	`waiting_approval` and `approvals` fields) — and a checkpoint of the rebound
1022	state is written at that same node boundary. The execution's state then
1023	carries the target version.
1024	
1025	Everything that follows uses the target version's definition: ready-node
1026	selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval points, retries, and
1027	the workflow subscriptions that fire for later events. Everything recorded
1028	before the migration is kept exactly as-is: prior events, node outputs,
1029	condition conclusions, and per-iteration history are never rewritten. Loops
1030	introduced by the target definition begin in their initial pending state; a
1031	loop the old definition knew keeps its recorded iterations and conclusion.
1032	Replay rebuilds the migration point and version binding solely from the
1033	event stream, and after a restart recovery continues on the migrated version
1034	from the migration checkpoint, so checkpoints and materialized state agree.
1035	
1036	An execution parked at an approval point may also be migrated: the waiting
1037	point keeps its recorded node and approver list unchanged (only a recorded
1038	approver may still decide it), and once the decision lands the subsequent
1039	advancement follows the target version. Executions that are never migrated
1040	keep advancing on the version they started with to completion or
1041	termination; adding versions never moves them. An execution of a workflow
1042	that never declared a version cannot name a target, and such workflows and
1043	their executions keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
1044	content.
1045	
1046	The response is the updated execution state. Migrating a `completed` or
1047	`terminated` execution returns `409 conflict` and changes nothing. A missing
1048	execution or a target version that does not exist for the workflow returns
1049	`404 not_found`; a cross-tenant reference is the same missing resource. A
1050	missing or mistyped `version`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
1051	`400 validation_error`. Migrating a running execution to the version it is
1052	already bound to returns the current state as-is, appending no event and
1053	writing no checkpoint; a `completed` or `terminated` execution instead
1054	returns `409 conflict` even when the target version is exactly the one it is
1055	bound to. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a `409
1056	conflict`. The migration event is listed directly by the per-execution
1057	events query, and node outputs produced after the migration belong to the
1058	target version's definition. Approver-list validation, lease renewal, and
1059	delivery history keep their existing semantics before and after a migration.
1060	
1061	### Start an execution
1062	
1063	```http
1064	POST /executions
1065	Idempotency-Key: execution-request-1
1066	
1067	{"id":"run-1","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{"order_id":"o-7"}}
1068	```
1069	
1070	Returns HTTP 201. The execution starts in `running` state. Without an
1071	explicit `version`, it binds to the workflow's current version at start time;
1072	naming a `version` binds to that one instead (and a missing version is a
1073	`404 not_found`). See "Workflow versions" for the binding and upgrade rules.
1074	
1075	An execution may declare a timeout:
1076	
1077	```json
1078	{"id":"run-2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{},"timeout_seconds":30}
1079	```
1080	
1081	`timeout_seconds` is a positive number of seconds counted from the moment the
1082	execution starts. Once the deadline passes, the execution terminates with
1083	termination reason `timeout` and no longer accepts output. Executions without
1084	a timeout never expire.
1085	
1086	An execution may also declare its own webhook `subscriptions`, which apply in
1087	addition to the ones its workflow declares:
1088	
1089	```json
1090	{
1091	  "id": "run-3",
1092	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
1093	  "input": {},
1094	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/ops", "events": ["node_completed"], "max_attempts": 3}]
1095	}
1096	```
1097	
1098	### List workflows
1099	
1100	```http
1101	GET /workflows?limit=50
1102	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1103	```
1104	
1105	Enumerates the workflows declared in the request's namespace. The response
1106	is `{"workflows":[{"id":"order-flow"}, ...]}`: one entry per workflow, each
1107	carrying its identifier, in ascending identifier order. A namespace with no
1108	workflows gets the definite empty result `{"workflows":[]}`, not an error.
1109	The query is read-only: it creates nothing, appends no events, and records
1110	no usage, so repeating it returns the same answer and changes no stored
1111	state.
1112	
1113	The list is paged with a keyset cursor:
1114	
1115	- `limit` — required; the maximum number of entries in the page, a positive
1116	  integer. The page never holds more entries than the limit;
1117	- `cursor` — optional; the identifier of the previous page's last entry.
1118	  Only entries whose identifier sorts strictly after the cursor are
1119	  returned, so paging with the previous page's last identifier yields
1120	  consecutive pages that neither overlap nor skip. A cursor past the end
1121	  returns the definite empty list.
1122	
1123	### List executions
1124	
1125	```http
1126	GET /executions?workflow_id=order-flow&status=terminated&termination_reason=timeout&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=run-41&limit=50
1127	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1128	```
1129	
1130	Enumerates the executions in the request's namespace in ascending execution
1131	identifier order. The response is `{"executions":[...]}`; each entry carries
1132	the execution `id`, its `workflow_id`, its `status` (`running`, `completed`,
1133	or `terminated`, always a string), its `termination_reason` (one of the
1134	four termination reasons for a terminated execution, otherwise `null`), and
1135	its `created_at` (the ISO-8601 UTC creation timestamp ending in `Z`), in
1136	that stable key order. A namespace with no executions gets the definite
1137	empty result `{"executions":[]}`. Like the workflows list this query is
1138	read-only and never settles a due timeout, appends an event, writes a
1139	checkpoint, or records usage, so repeated calls return the same answer and
1140	change no state or metering conclusion.
1141	
1142	The same `limit` and `cursor` pagination applies, with the cursor taken
1143	from the previous page's last execution identifier. In addition, five
1144	filters may be combined, and every given filter must match:
1145	
1146	- `workflow_id` — only executions of that workflow. Referencing a workflow
1147	  the namespace does not contain, including one owned by another tenant, is
1148	  the usual `404 not_found` and reveals nothing about its existence;
1149	- `status` — only executions in that lifecycle status. A value other than
1150	  `running`, `completed`, or `terminated` is a `400 validation_error`;
1151	- `termination_reason` — only executions that terminated for exactly that
1152	  reason. The filter is meaningful solely for terminated executions:
1153	  running and completed executions never appear under it, even when other
1154	  filters are given alongside it. An unknown reason is a
1155	  `400 validation_error`;
1156	- `since` and `until` — the same closed creation-time bounds the events and
1157	  metrics queries accept: each is an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp ending in `Z`,
1158	  and an execution whose `created_at` equals `since` or `until` is
1159	  returned. When either parameter is absent the corresponding bound is
1160	  open, so omitting both returns exactly the unfiltered list; a malformed
1161	  timestamp is a `400 validation_error`. When `since` is later than
1162	  `until` the window matches nothing and the result is the definite empty
1163	  list, not an error.
1164	
1165	Both list endpoints follow the usual tenant scope: omitting
1166	`X-Tenant-Id` keeps the single legacy namespace, and a tenant sees only its
1167	own workflows and executions under every combination of filters. Every
1168	parameter may appear at most once; a repeated parameter, an unknown
1169	parameter, a missing `limit`, or a `limit` that is not a positive integer is
1170	a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing.
1171	
1172	### Inspect an execution
1173	
1174	```http
1175	GET /executions/run-1
1176	GET /executions/run-1/events
1177	GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
1178	```
1179	
1180	The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
1181	ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
1182	gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
1183	`state` summary, and `created_at`.
1184	
1185	The events query is read-only: it appends no events, records no usage, and
1186	changes no state, so advancement, approvals, recovery, and replay never alter
1187	what it observes. With no query parameters it returns the complete ordered
1188	event list exactly as before. It also accepts optional filter and pagination
1189	parameters, which combine as an intersection:
1190	
1191	```http
1192	GET /executions/run-1/events?types=node_completed,node_failed&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
1193	```
1194	
1195	- `types` — a comma-separated set of event types; only events whose type is
1196	  in the set are returned. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown
1197	  event type is a `400 validation_error`;
1198	- `since` and `until` — the same closed-interval occurrence-time bounds the
1199	  metrics query accepts: an event whose time equals either boundary is
1200	  returned. When `since` is later than `until` the window matches nothing and
1201	  the result is an empty list, not an error;
1202	- `cursor` — the sequence of the last event of the previous page; only events
1203	  with a strictly greater sequence are returned;
1204	- `limit` — the maximum number of events in the page, in ascending sequence
1205	  order.
1206	
1207	Every parameter may appear at most once; a repeated parameter, an unknown
1208	parameter, a malformed timestamp, or a cursor or limit that is not a positive
1209	integer is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Filtering never
1210	renumbers events, so paging with `cursor` set to the previous page's last
1211	sequence yields consecutive pages that neither overlap nor skip. A filter
1212	that matches nothing returns the definite empty result `{"events":[]}`, and
1213	querying a missing or another tenant's execution is the usual
1214	`404 not_found`.
1215	
1216	### Webhook notifications
1217	
1218	Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
1219	messages when business events occur. Each webhook subscription contains exactly:
1220	
1221	- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
1222	- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
1223	  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
1224	  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
1225	  reason);
1226	- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
1227	  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
1228	- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.
1229	
1230	Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
1231	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
1232	a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
1233	ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
1234	workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written. A subscription
1235	may instead declare a queue target (`queue` instead of `url`); see "Queue
1236	subscriptions" below.
1237	
1238	When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
1239	target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
1240	event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
1241	approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
1242	header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
1243	never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
1244	`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
1245	unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
1246	failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
1247	triggered it.
1248	
1249	Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
1250	state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
1251	checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
1252	no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
1253	results as before.
1254	
1255	### Inspect the delivery history
1256	
1257	```http
1258	GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
1259	```
1260	
1261	Returns `{"deliveries": [...]}` in the order the events occurred. Each record
1262	gives its `sequence`, the subscription `url`, the `event_type`, the
1263	`event_sequence` that triggered it, the delivery `idempotency_key`, the final
1264	`status` (`delivered` or `failed`), the `attempt_count`, an `attempts` list
1265	recording each try's `status_code` or `error` (so a retry that eventually
1266	succeeds is visible attempt by attempt), and `occurred_at`. Querying the
1267	history of a missing execution returns 404 `not_found` and records nothing.
1268	Every delivery attempt is recorded, including one whose history record itself
1269	could not be written: such a failure is not swallowed — it is retried once in
1270	a fresh write carrying `status` `failed` and a `persistence_error` describing
1271	the write failure, so the attempt remains visible whenever the database can
1272	accept it (and is logged rather than silently dropped if it cannot).
1273	
1274	### Queue subscriptions
1275	
1276	A subscription may declare a queue target instead of a webhook `url`:
1277	
1278	```json
1279	{
1280	  "id": "run-4",
1281	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
1282	  "input": {},
1283	  "subscriptions": [{"queue": "order-events", "events": ["node_completed"], "visibility_seconds": 60}]
1284	}
1285	```
1286	
1287	A queue subscription contains exactly:
1288	
1289	- `queue`: a non-empty queue name of any length;
1290	- `events`: the same non-empty event-type list a webhook subscription takes;
1291	- `visibility_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds a pulled
1292	  message stays invisible while awaiting acknowledgement, defaulting to 30.
1293	
1294	Exactly one of `url` and `queue` must be present in a subscription. Any
1295	other field, a missing or invalid `events` list, an empty queue name, or a
1296	non-positive or non-finite visibility timeout is a 400 `validation_error`
1297	that rejects the whole request without partial writes. Queue names are
1298	unique per tenant across declarations: declaring a name that another
1299	workflow or execution of the same tenant already declared is a 409
1300	`conflict`, while different tenants may reuse the same names freely.
1301	
1302	A workflow or an execution may declare several queue targets. Every
1303	execution gets its own queues — those declared on the workflow revision it
1304	is bound to, plus those it declares itself — and when a subscribed event
1305	occurs, a message carrying the event type and its details is appended to
1306	each matching queue of that execution, in occurrence order. The append is
1307	atomic with the event itself: a rejected operation leaves no queued message
1308	behind. Each message carries an idempotency key that is deterministic per
1309	event and queue: every delivery of the same message reuses the same key,
1310	and different events never share a key. Queues add no fields to the
1311	execution state and append no events, and replay, recovery, and queries
1312	never enqueue. Executions that declare no queue targets behave exactly as
1313	before.
1314	
1315	### Inspect the queue state
1316	
1317	```http
1318	GET /executions/run-4/queues
1319	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1320	```
1321	
1322	Returns `{"queues": [...]}` with one entry per queue of the execution, in
1323	declaration order; an execution with no queue targets gets the definite
1324	empty result `{"queues": []}`. Each entry gives its `queue` name, the
1325	`visibility_seconds` in effect, and the queue's `messages` in entry order —
1326	an empty list for a queue that never received a message. Each message record
1327	gives its `sequence` (the entry order), the `event_type` and
1328	`event_sequence` that produced it, the event `payload`, the message
1329	`idempotency_key`, the `delivery_count`, a `deliveries` list recording every
1330	delivery with its `delivery` number and `delivered_at` time, the
1331	`enqueued_at` time, and the current `status` (`pending`, `delivered`, or
1332	`acknowledged`). Querying the queues of a missing execution — including one
1333	owned by another tenant — is the usual 404 `not_found`.
1334	
1335	### Pull messages from a queue
1336	
1337	```http
1338	POST /executions/run-4/queues/order-events/pull
1339	Idempotency-Key: pull-request-1
1340	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1341	
1342	{}
1343	```
1344	
1345	The body must be an empty object. The response is `{"messages": [...]}`: the
1346	currently pending messages in entry order, each rendered like the message
1347	records of the queue state query. A pulled message becomes invisible for the
1348	queue's visibility timeout; if it is not acknowledged by then, it returns to
1349	the pending set and is delivered again — the queue semantics are at least
1350	once, and every delivery is recorded in the message's delivery history.
1351	Pulling an empty queue, or one whose messages are all invisible, is a
1352	definite empty result `{"messages": []}`, not an error. Every delivery to
1353	the caller is metered as one `delivery_attempted` usage record, exactly like
1354	an outbound webhook attempt, and counts toward the tenant's bill.
1355	
1356	### Acknowledge a message
1357	
1358	```http
1359	POST /executions/run-4/queues/order-events/ack
1360	Idempotency-Key: ack-request-1

1371	Pulling from or acknowledging a queue the execution does not have, or one

1378	### Schedules

1416	
1417	### Declare or replace a schedule
1418	
1419	```http

1422

1432	
1433	### Inspect the schedule status
1434

1436	GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
